title: The chickpea
hookLine: a chickpea leaps out of the pot, and the cook explains the boiling makes it good (Masnavi 3)
tomorrow: a lion, a hare, a well. how does the small one win?

lines: A CHICKPEA LEAPS FOR THE RIM.
cards: Anyone who's cooked dried chickpeas for chana or hummus knows the long boil, and the foam, and the way a few of them bob up to the top as if they want out. Rumi watched that pot.
In his story a chickpea leaps toward the rim, trying to escape the boiling water, and the cook knocks it back down with the ladle. So why would a chickpea try to jump out? Because it hurts.
And what the cook says next opens an old, friendly argument about hard times.

teach.h: I'M NOT DOING THIS IN HATE.
teach.b: The cook, paraphrased: boil well. I'm not doing this because you're hateful to me. I'm doing it so you'll gain flavor and become food, mixed into life.
In the garden you drank the rain; now comes the fire. Two honest views grow from that pot. The first view reads hardship as cooking.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: EVEN A THORN COUNTS.
teach.b: It has a hadith in al-Bukhari behind it: no tiredness, illness, worry, grief or harm reaches a Muslim, not even the prick of a thorn, without God wiping away some of their sins by it.
Its best point: pain isn't wasted, and it isn't a sign God is angry. Cooked, not punished.
The second view pushes back on making suffering sound good.
It has its own hadith: the Prophet, peace be upon him, taught people to ask God for afiya, well-being, and al-Bukhari also keeps his words that God sent down no disease without also sending its cure.
He told people not to wish for death because of a harm that struck them. Its best point: you're allowed, even encouraged, to ask for ease, see the doctor, and leave the pot if you can.
Notice the chickpea didn't choose the boil, and nobody in the story tells it to jump in. Both views agree on that.

teach.h: MEANING IN THE HEAT, OR AN END TO IT.
teach.b: They differ on where to put the weight: on finding meaning inside the heat, or on asking for the heat to end.
It's possible to hold both: pray for afiya, and trust the cooking you can't escape.

how: Muslims facing illness or loss are taught both to be patient, trusting that hardship isn't wasted, and to ask God for afiya, well-being, and seek treatment, as the hadith encourage.

o: a punishment proving that God is angry with you
hardship as cooking that makes you good, not a penalty
a test you pass only by never complaining at all

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: wipes away some sins, says al-Bukhari

s: Islam teaches you should look for suffering, to be purified by it
the Prophet taught people to ask for afiya and to seek cures. nobody tells the chickpea to jump in.
a hadith in al-Bukhari says even a thorn's prick can wipe away some sins
the first view's anchor: pain isn't wasted.
in Rumi's story, the cook boils the chickpea out of anger
'I'm not doing this because you're hateful to me,' the cook says.

games.q: you lean toward 'hard times cook us.' a friend says, 'no: pray for ease and get help.' state her side at its best.
o: the Prophet taught people to ask for well-being and to seek cures.
suffering never has any meaning, so don't look for one.
asking God for ease shows that your faith is weak.
games.why: her view has its own hadith: ask for afiya; no disease without a cure; don't wish for death over a harm. both views agree nobody should jump into the pot.

practice: Close your eyes and sit without shifting for the whole sit. When an itch or an ache asks you to move, notice it, breathe once into it, and let it stay one breath longer before you settle. Small heat, small cooking.

wordCard.voice: The chickpea: Rumi's story of a chickpea leaping from the pot, and the cook who says the boiling isn't hatred but making it good.

orig.note: Arabic: well-being, safety from harm; what the Prophet taught people to ask God for.

carryVoice: For the long-boil weeks: cooked, not punished, and still free to ask for ease. Six of Rumi's eight stories told.

sources.ref: Rumi, Masnavi, Book 3 (the chickpea and the cook)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5641–5642 (no fatigue, illness, worry or grief, even a thorn, without expiation of sins)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5678 (God sent down no disease without sending its cure)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5671 (do not wish for death because of a harm that befalls you)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi, book of supplications (ask God for pardon and afiya)
